title: Inside the Pentagon's AI war machine | GZERO World with Ian Bremmer
summary: Ian Bremmer and Katrina Manson on Project Maven: how the Pentagon put AI into targeting, autonomous weapons in development, and the risks of speed, error and civilian harm.

assertions.quote: The Pentagon is reporting using AI to generate hundreds of strike options in Iran

verdicts.note: Maven Smart System is in wide use for target identification and prioritization, as officials have described publicly.

assertions.quote: With the help of AI, they took humans out of three of those places on that cycle.

verdicts.note: US demonstrations and Israeli practice show human steps cut or reduced to supervision, though final strike approval formally stays with humans.

assertions.quote: We see autonomous drones and ground vehicles in the front lines in Ukraine

verdicts.note: Estonian intelligence reports Ukraine's commander saying drones cause up to 70% of equipment losses and Russia building a dedicated unmanned systems branch, which shows drones transforming warfare, but it describes mass-produced unmanned systems, not autonomy or swarms.
Danish intelligence says the war in Ukraine has highlighted the critical role of drones in modern warfare, supporting the transformation but saying nothing about autonomy or swarms.

ODNI says remotely operated or autonomous weapons proliferating in Ukraine have cut tactical adaptation cycles to weeks and uncrewed systems are already ubiquitous, enabling real-time targeting with AI, which supports drones transforming warfare but says nothing of swarms and mixes remote piloting with autonomy.

SIPRI notes the widespread use of drones, uncrewed underwater vehicles and loitering munitions in the Russia-Ukraine war and AI-guided drones hitting Russian strategic assets, but it does not show they are transforming warfare overall.

WEF says both sides in Russia's war on Ukraine have pushed the use of AI, with roles in geospatial intelligence, autonomous systems and cyber warfare; it supports growing autonomy but says nothing of swarms or a transformation.

assertions.quote: once you have an autonomous weaponized vehicle, you don't need to worry about jamming.

verdicts.note: CNAS notes one reason for autonomy is letting uninhabited vehicles continue missions without reliable communication links to their controllers, which is the mechanism behind the claim, though it does not discuss jamming itself.

assertions.quote: Sure, humans make mistakes, but AI could potentially make many more, much faster and at scale.

verdicts.note: Automated systems can repeat an error across many targets quickly, but comparative error rates against human targeting are not public.

assertions.quote: the U.S. military thinks they are further ahead at adoption, at practicing the workflows, and at actual combat experience.

verdicts.note: Neither side publishes its assessment, and China's military AI adoption is opaque.

assertions.quote: I hate to admit it, but AI atrocities are possible in this new era.

verdicts.note: Evidence is contested: reporting on AI-assisted targeting in Gaza suggests higher civilian harm, but no controlled comparison exists.
SIPRI reports Chinese experts' concern that AI could increase collateral damage among other risks, an expert opinion not backed by data here.
